catalog_quote: Mead 1998:96-97 (sec. 3.1.2 Syllable patterns and stress): 'The syllable patterns reconstructed for Proto-Bungku-Tolaki are V(C) and CV(C), with a coda possible only in word-final position—in other words no consonant clusters were possible word-medially. ... I assume that in Proto-Bungku-Tolaki stress fell on the penultimate syllable, there being no reason to reconstruct otherwise. All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages also exhibit penultimate stress.' Mead 1999:101-102 (Appendix 3, selected word lists, Waru = WAR included): '(g) In the absence of any stress marking, one can assume penultimate stress occurring on the next to last written vowel. ... (d) None of the Bungku-Tolaki languages have phonemically long vowels. Phonetically long vowels are nearly always a reflection of two vowels of the same quality, and have been transcribed as such in the following data ... All of the Bungku-…

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: both deciding passages (Mead 1998:97; Mead 1999:101-102) are verbatim in held files at the stated places, and the held PL-D91 text confirms Waru is inside the scope of Mead's first-hand survey (lists 61-62, elicited by Mead, 'very good'). The classification (fixed penultimate) rests on a family-level statement in a 1998 comparative dissertation rather than a Waru-specific description, but no Waru-specific description exists (Glottolog: 0 descriptive refs; MED wordlist-or-less), so the held sources are the best available and nothing suggests the coding is wrong.
